title: Concilium deorum
titleEn: The Council of the Gods — Aeneid X.1–95
about: The opening of Book X. While the Trojan camp is still under siege and Aeneas is away seeking allies, Jupiter throws open the halls of Olympus and calls the gods to council. He rebukes them for their quarrelling: he had forbidden Italy to fight the Trojans, and the proper time for war will come only when Carthage pours over the Alps against Rome; for now they are to make peace. Venus answers at length. She complains that Turnus rides in triumph, that the Rutulians are inside the Trojan walls, that a second Troy is besieged and Diomedes is roused again; she lists Juno's past attacks, the storm, the burning of the ships, the Fury Allecto let loose on Italy; she gives up all hope of empire and asks only that Ascanius may be spared and live out his days in obscurity in one of her shrines; if the Trojans are not to have Italy, they might as well go back to the ashes of Troy. Juno, stung into speech, throws Venus's words back at her: Aeneas chose war and left his camp of his own will; Turnus has a right to fight on his own soil; Venus herself has worked miracles for the Trojans; and the whole Trojan war began with Venus's own favourite, Paris, and his theft of Helen. It is too late, she says, for complaints.

sentences.t:
Panditur interea domus omnipotentis Olympi,
conciliumque vocat divom pater atque hominum rex
sideream in sedem, terras unde arduus omnis
castraque Dardanidum adspectat populosque Latinos.
sentences.l:
Thrown open meanwhile is the house of all-powerful Olympus,
and calls a council the father of gods and king of men
into his starry seat, from where, on high, all the lands
and the camp of the Dardanians he looks on, and the Latin peoples.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the halls of almighty Olympus are thrown open, and the father of the gods and king of men summons a council to his starry seat, from whose height he looks down on every land, on the Dardan camp and on the peoples of Latium.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. Book X opens here, and it opens in heaven: after the long siege of Book IX the poem rises to a council of the gods, as the Iliad does at the start of Books 4 and 8; in Book 8 Zeus calls the gods together and forbids them to join the fighting. 'Panditur', 'is thrown open', the doors of heaven swinging wide. 'divom pater atque hominum rex', 'father of gods and king of men', an old formula going back to Ennius; 'divom' = 'divorum'. 'unde', 'from where', is held back behind 'terras'. 'arduus', 'on high', describes Jupiter himself. 'adspectat' is Greenough's spelling of 'aspectat', 'gazes on'. 'Dardanidum', 'of the Dardanians', the Trojans, sons of Dardanus. Elisions 'atqu(e) hominum', 'sidere(am) in', 'und(e) arduus', 'Dardanid(um) adspectat'.

sentences.t: Considunt tectis bipatentibus, incipit ipse:
sentences.l: They take their seats in the hall with double doors; he himself begins:
sentences.i: They sit down in the hall whose doors stand open on either side, and he himself begins:
sentences.n: 'Considunt', 'they sit down', the gods taking their places. 'tectis bipatentibus', 'in the hall opening on two sides', a local ablative; 'bipatens', a rare compound, describes double doors standing open front and back. 'incipit ipse', 'he himself begins', Jupiter, who speaks first as the president of the council. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Caelicolae magni, quianam sententia vobis
versa retro tantumque animis certatis iniquis?
sentences.l:
“Heaven-dwellers great, why is your judgement
turned back, and so much with hostile minds do you contend?
sentences.i: “Great dwellers in heaven, why have you turned your judgement back, and why do you strive with one another in so bitter a spirit?
sentences.n: Jupiter's speech begins. 'Caelicolae', 'heaven-dwellers', an epic compound. 'quianam', three syllables, qui-a-nam, an archaic word for 'why', from the old Latin of Ennius, fitting the solemn occasion. 'sententia vobis versa retro', 'your opinion turned backwards', 'vobis' a dative of reference. Jupiter speaks as if the gods had accepted his will and gone back on it; the poem shows no such scene, and commentators have remarked on it. 'tantum', 'so much', adverbial accusative. 'animis… iniquis', 'with unfriendly minds', ablative of manner. Elision 'tantumqu(e) animis'.

sentences.t: Abnueram bello Italiam concurrere Teucris.
sentences.l: I had forbidden Italy to clash in war with the Teucrians.
sentences.i: I had refused my consent for Italy to meet the Trojans in war.
sentences.n: 'Abnueram', 'I had refused', pluperfect: the refusal came before all this fighting. 'abnuo', literally to shake the head in refusal, takes the accusative and infinitive 'Italiam concurrere', 'that Italy should clash'. 'bello', 'in war', ablative. 'Teucris', dative with 'concurrere': the Trojans, named after Teucer, an early king of the Troad (you'll see 'Teucri' constantly). Elision 'bell(o) Italiam'.

sentences.t: Quae contra vetitum discordia?
sentences.l: What, against my ban, is this discord?
sentences.i: What strife is this, in defiance of my prohibition?
sentences.n: 'Quae… discordia?', 'what discord (is this)?', the verb left out, as often in an angry question. 'contra vetitum', 'against what was forbidden', 'vetitum' the neuter participle of 'veto' used as a noun, 'the prohibition'. The short question, less than a line long, has the sharpness of a ruler calling the room to order. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quis metus aut hos
aut hos arma sequi ferrumque lacessere suasit?
sentences.l:
What fear either these
or these to follow arms and to provoke the steel persuaded?
sentences.i: What fear has driven one side or the other to take up arms and challenge the sword?
sentences.n: 'aut hos aut hos', 'either these or those', the two sides, Trojans and Latins, named by the same pronoun twice across the line end. 'Quis metus', 'what fear', as if each side could only have fought out of fear of the other. 'suasit' takes the infinitives 'sequi' and 'lacessere', 'persuaded (them) to follow… to provoke'. 'ferrum lacessere', 'to challenge the steel', to start armed conflict. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Adveniet iustum pugnae, ne arcessite, tempus,
cum fera Karthago Romanis arcibus olim
exitium magnum atque Alpes immittet apertas:
sentences.l:
There will come the right time for battle — do not summon it —
when fierce Carthage upon the Roman citadels one day
great destruction, and the Alps laid open, shall let loose:
sentences.i: The proper time for fighting will come — do not hasten it — when one day fierce Carthage will open the Alps and hurl great ruin upon the strongholds of Rome:
sentences.n: 'iustum… tempus', 'the right time', enclosing 'pugnae, ne arcessite', with 'pugnae' as genitive. 'ne arcessite', 'do not call it in', 'ne' with the imperative, an old and poetic form of prohibition (prose uses 'noli' with the infinitive). Jupiter looks ahead to the Second Punic War, when Hannibal led a Carthaginian army over the Alps into Italy (218 BCE): 'Alpes immittet apertas', 'shall send in the Alps opened', a bold way of saying the passes will be breached and an army poured through them. 'Romanis arcibus', dative with 'immittet'. 'Karthago', with Greenough's K. Elisions 'n(e) arcessite', 'magn(um) atque', 'atqu(e) Alpes'.

sentences.t: tum certare odiis, tum res rapuisse licebit.
sentences.l: then to contend with hatreds, then to have seized things will be allowed.
sentences.i: Then there will be leave for hatred to strive with hatred, and for plunder.
sentences.n: 'tum… tum', anaphora: then, and only then. 'certare odiis', 'to contend with hatreds', ablative of means. 'res rapuisse', 'to have seized goods', to plunder; the perfect infinitive here names the plain act, with no sense of past time, a common licence of verse after verbs of permission and the like. 'licebit', 'it will be permitted'. Elision 'certar(e) odiis'.

sentences.t: Nunc sinite et placitum laeti componite foedus.”
sentences.l: Now let it be, and the approved compact gladly settle.”
sentences.i: For now let it rest, and with good grace make the peace that I approve.”
sentences.n: Jupiter's speech ends here, ten lines, short and imperious. 'sinite', 'let (it) be', leave off. 'placitum… foedus', 'the treaty that pleases (me)', 'placitum' a participle of 'placeo', 'agreed, approved'. 'laeti', 'glad', the adjective doing an adverb's work: make peace cheerfully. 'componite', 'settle, put together'. Elision 'sinit(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter haec paucis; at non Venus aurea contra
pauca refert:
sentences.l:
Jupiter these things in few words; but not golden Venus in reply
few things returns:
sentences.i: So Jupiter spoke, in few words; but golden Venus answered with words that were not few:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Iuppiter haec paucis', 'Jupiter (said) this in few words', the verb of speaking left out, as often. 'non… pauca', 'not few', litotes for 'many': the play on 'paucis… pauca' sets her long speech against his short one. 'aurea', 'golden', Homer's epithet for Aphrodite. 'contra', 'in reply'. 'pauca refert' is a half-line, one of those left unfinished at Virgil's death; the text keeps it as it is. No elisions.

sentences.t: “O pater, O hominum rerumque aeterna potestas!
sentences.l: “O father, O of men and of things the eternal power!
sentences.i: “Father, everlasting power over men and over all the world!
sentences.n: Venus's speech begins, with a solemn address. 'O… O', the interjection, repeated, and not elided before the vowel of 'hominum'. 'hominum rerumque aeterna potestas', 'eternal power of men and things', the abstract noun 'potestas' standing for the one who wields it, as a title of majesty. Venus is Jupiter's daughter, so 'pater' is literal as well as formal. Elision 'rerumqu(e) aeterna'.

sentences.t: Namque aliud quid sit, quod iam implorare queamus?
sentences.l: For what else could there be, which now we could implore?
sentences.i: For what other power is left that we could now call on for help?
sentences.n: 'Namque', 'for', explains the address: she turns to him because there is no one else. 'aliud quid sit', 'what else could there be', a potential subjunctive in a question. 'quod… queamus', a relative clause of characteristic, 'such that we could implore it'; 'queo', 'I am able'. 'implorare', 'to call on with tears', to beg for help. Elisions 'Namqu(e) aliud', 'i(am) implorare'.

sentences.t:
[Cernis ut insultent Rutulli Turnusque feratur]
[per medios insignis equis tumidusque secundo]
Marte ruat?
sentences.l:
[Do you see how the Rutulians exult, and Turnus is borne]
[through the midst, conspicuous on his horses, and swollen with favouring]
war he charges on?
sentences.i: Do you see how the Rutulians mock us, and how Turnus rides through the thick of them, splendid with his horses, and storms on, swollen with pride at his success in war?
sentences.n: The print has 'Rutulli', a misprint for 'Rutuli', corrected here. Greenough prints lines 20 and 21 inside square brackets, marking them as doubtful; we keep them as he prints them and translate them, since the question cannot stand without them. 'Cernis ut', 'do you see how', 'ut' introducing indirect questions in the subjunctive: 'insultent… feratur… ruat'. 'insultent', 'leap upon, exult over' a fallen enemy. 'insignis equis', 'conspicuous with his horses', his chariot team. 'tumidus secundo Marte', 'swollen with favouring Mars', Mars put for war itself. No elisions.

sentences.t: Non clausa tegunt iam moenia Teucros:
sentences.l: Not do closed walls protect now the Teucrians:
sentences.i: Their walls are shut, yet no longer give the Trojans shelter:
sentences.n: 'Non clausa tegunt iam moenia', 'the walls, though shut, no longer protect', 'clausa' concessive in force: the gates are barred, and still the enemy is inside. Venus is describing the end of Book IX, where Turnus was shut inside the camp and fought his way out. 'Teucros', the Trojans. No elisions.

sentences.t:
quin intra portas atque ipsis proelia miscent
aggeribus moerorum et inundant sanguine fossas.
sentences.l:
nay, within the gates and on the very
ramparts of the walls they join battle, and flood with blood the trenches.
sentences.i: they are fighting inside the gates, on the very ramparts of the walls, and drenching the trenches in blood.
sentences.n: 'quin', 'nay more', capping the last statement. 'ipsis… aggeribus moerorum', 'on the very earthworks of the walls'; 'moerorum' is Greenough's archaic spelling of 'murorum'. 'proelia miscent', 'they mingle battles', they join battle, a common epic phrase. The Latin Library prints 'fossae' for 'fossas': then the trenches are the subject, 'and the trenches overflow with blood'; Greenough's 'fossas' keeps the Rutulians as subject, flooding the trenches. Elisions 'atqu(e) ipsis', 'moeror(um) et'.

sentences.t: Aeneas ignarus abest.
sentences.l: Aeneas, unknowing, is away.
sentences.i: Aeneas is away and knows nothing of it.
sentences.n: A short, bare sentence that Juno will throw back at Venus word for word in line 85. Aeneas has gone up the Tiber to seek allies from Evander and the Etruscans (Book VIII) and does not know of the attack. 'ignarus', 'not knowing', describes him in his absence. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Numquamne levari
obsidione sines?
sentences.l:
Never will you let them be relieved
of the siege?
sentences.i: Will you never let them be freed from siege?
sentences.n: 'Numquamne… sines', 'will you never allow', '-ne' attached to the first word of a question. 'levari', 'to be relieved', passive infinitive with 'sines'; the Trojans are understood as its subject. 'obsidione', ablative of separation, 'from the siege'. The word looks back to Troy's ten-year siege, now beginning again in Italy, as the next lines say. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Muris iterum imminet hostis
[nascentis Troiae nec non exercitus alter;]
sentences.l:
Over the walls again hangs an enemy
[of Troy being born, and a second army too;]
sentences.i: Once more an enemy looms over the walls of a Troy only just being born, once more a second army;
sentences.n: Greenough prints line 27 inside square brackets as doubtful; we keep it and translate it. 'Muris… imminet', 'hangs over the walls', 'muris' dative with the compound verb. 'iterum', 'again', is the key word: Troy is besieged a second time. 'nascentis Troiae', 'of Troy being born', the Trojan camp in Italy seen as the new Troy. 'nec non', 'and also', two negatives making a positive. 'exercitus alter', 'a second army', like the Greek host before the old Troy. Elision 'iter(um) imminet'.

sentences.t:
atque iterum in Teucros Aetolis surgit ab Arpis
Tydides.
sentences.l:
and again against the Teucrians from Aetolian Arpi rises
the son of Tydeus.
sentences.i: and once again Diomedes rises against the Trojans, this time from Aetolian Arpi.
sentences.n: 'Tydides', 'son of Tydeus', is Diomedes, one of the fiercest Greeks at Troy, who after the war settled in Apulia and founded Arpi; 'Aetolis', 'Aetolian', because his father Tydeus came from Aetolia. In Book VIII the Latins sent an envoy to ask his help; Venus speaks as if he were already on the march. The name is held over to the next line for effect. Elisions 'atqu(e) iterum', 'iter(um) in'.

sentences.t:
Equidem credo, mea volnera restant
et tua progenies mortalia demoror arma.
sentences.l:
Truly I believe, my wounds remain,
and I, your offspring, wait for mortal arms.
sentences.i: Indeed I believe my own wounds are still to come, and I, your daughter, am only waiting for the weapons of mortals.
sentences.n: In Iliad 5 Diomedes wounded Aphrodite in the hand as she carried Aeneas out of the fight, and she fled weeping to Olympus. Venus says bitterly that another wound awaits her. 'Equidem', 'for my part, truly'. 'mea volnera restant', 'my wounds remain', are still in store; 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera'. 'tua progenies', 'your offspring', in apposition to the 'I' of 'demoror'. 'demoror', 'I wait for', I am kept waiting for. No elisions.

sentences.i: If the Trojans have made for Italy without your sanction and against your divine will, let them pay for their offences, and give them no help;
sentences.n: Venus sets out two cases: 'Si… sin', 'if… but if'. 'sine pace tua', 'without your peace', your favour or leave, 'pax' in its old religious sense of the gods' goodwill. 'invito numine', ablative absolute, 'your divine will being unwilling'. 'petiere' = 'petierunt' (the '-ere' perfect again). 'luant', jussive subjunctive, 'let them atone for'. 'neque… iuveris', 'and do not help', the perfect subjunctive in a prohibition. Elisions 'tu(a) atque', 'atqu(e) invito', 'nequ(e) illos'.

sentences.t:
sin tot responsa secuti,
quae superi manesque dabant: cur nunc tua quisquam
vertere iussa potest aut cur nova condere fata?
sentences.l:
but if, having followed so many oracles
which those above and the shades were giving: why now your
commands can anyone overturn, or why new fates establish?
sentences.i: but if they have obeyed all the oracles given them by the gods above and by the shades below, why can anyone now overturn your commands, or why found a new order of fate?
sentences.n: 'sin… secuti', 'but if (they have) followed', 'sunt' left out, and the sentence breaks off into a question after the colon. 'responsa', 'answers', oracles: the gods above spoke through Apollo and the Penates, the 'manes', the spirits of the dead, through Anchises' ghost in Book VI. 'tua quisquam vertere iussa', 'anyone… to overturn your orders', 'tua… iussa' framing the subject. 'quisquam', 'anyone', is Juno, not named. 'nova condere fata', 'to found new destinies'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quid repetem exustas Erycino in litore classes,
quid tempestatum regem ventosque furentis
Aeolia excitos aut actam nubibus Irim?
sentences.l:
Why should I recall the burned fleet on the Erycine shore,
why the king of storms and the winds raging
roused out of Aeolia, or Iris driven through the clouds?
sentences.i: Why should I go back over the ships burned on the shore by Eryx, or the king of the storms and his raging winds called up out of Aeolia, or Iris sent racing through the clouds?
sentences.n: The print has 'repetem', a misprint for 'repetam', corrected here: 'Quid repetam', 'why should I recall', is a deliberative subjunctive. Venus lists Juno's attacks: in Book V Iris, sent by Juno, stirred the Trojan women to burn the ships in Sicily, near Mount Eryx; in Book I Juno had Aeolus, king of the winds, raise the storm. 'Aeolia', 'from Aeolia', his island, ablative of place from which. 'Irim', accusative; 'actam nubibus', 'driven through the clouds'. 'classes', plural for the one fleet. 'furentis', accusative plural in '-is'. Elisions 'repet(am) exustas', 'Erycin(o) in', 'Aeoli(a) excitos'.

sentences.t:
Nunc etiam manis, haec intemptata manebat
sors rerum, movet et superis immissa repente
Allecto, medias Italum bacchata per urbes.
sentences.l:
Now even the shades — this untried remained
share of the world — she stirs, and upon those above suddenly let loose
Allecto through the midst of the Italians' cities has raged like a Bacchant.
sentences.i: Now she is stirring up even the dead — that was the one region of the world still left untried — and Allecto, suddenly let loose upon the world above, has gone raving like a Bacchant through the cities of Italy.
sentences.n: In Book VII Juno, unable to bend the gods above, summoned the Fury Allecto from the underworld to rouse the Latins to war ('flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo'). 'manis', accusative plural in '-is', 'the shades'. 'haec intemptata manebat sors rerum', 'this lot of the world remained untried', the underworld as the third share of the universe. 'movet', the subject is best taken as Juno, unnamed, as her own words in Book VII suggest (some make it Allecto). 'superis', dative, 'upon the upper world'. 'Italum' = 'Italorum'. 'bacchata', 'having raved like a Bacchant', '(est)' understood. No elisions.

sentences.t: Nil super imperio moveor:
sentences.l: Not at all about empire am I moved:
sentences.i: For empire I care nothing now:
sentences.n: 'Nil', 'not at all', adverbial. 'super imperio', 'about empire', 'super' with the ablative meaning 'concerning', a poetic use. In Book I Jupiter promised Venus an empire without end for Aeneas's descendants; now she says she will give it up. 'moveor', 'I am moved, troubled'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
speravimus ista,
dum fortuna fuit;
sentences.l:
we hoped for those things
while fortune was;
sentences.i: we hoped for that while fortune still stood by us;
sentences.n: 'speravimus', 'we hoped', the plural used for herself, as goddesses often speak; the perfect implies the hope is over. 'ista', 'those things', the empire just named, with a touch of scorn for what is now out of reach. 'dum fortuna fuit', 'while there was fortune', while our good fortune lasted. No elisions.

sentences.t: vincant quos vincere mavis.
sentences.l: let those win whom to win you prefer.
sentences.i: let those conquer whom you would rather see conquer.
sentences.n: 'vincant', jussive subjunctive, 'let them win'. 'quos vincere mavis', 'whom you prefer to win', 'mavis' from 'malo' (= 'magis volo'). The repetition 'vincant… vincere' gives her resignation a bitter edge: she does not say whom she means, but everyone knows. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Si nulla est regio, Teucris quam det tua coniunx
dura, per eversae, genitor, fumantia Troiae
exscidia obtestor, liceat dimittere ab armis
incolumem Ascanium, liceat superesse nepotem.
sentences.l:
If there is no region which to the Teucrians your wife would give,
harsh as she is, by the overthrown, father, smoking, of Troy
ruins I beseech you, let it be allowed to send away from arms
unharmed Ascanius, let it be allowed my grandson to survive.
sentences.i: If there is no country your unbending wife will grant the Trojans, then, father, by the smoking ruins of fallen Troy I implore you, let me take Ascanius out of the fighting unharmed, let my grandson at least survive.
sentences.n: 'quam det', a relative clause of characteristic, 'which she would give'. 'tua coniunx dura', 'your harsh wife', Juno, named only by this sneer, 'dura' held over to the next line for weight. 'per… exscidia obtestor', 'I beseech you by the ruins', the words framing 'genitor' and 'fumantia'; 'exscidia' is Greenough's spelling of 'excidia'. 'liceat… liceat', anaphora, 'may it be allowed'. 'nepotem', 'grandson', Ascanius, Aeneas's son. Elisions 'null(a) est', 'exscidi(a) obtestor', 'dimitter(e) ab', 'incolum(em) Ascanium'.

sentences.t:
Aeneas sane ignotis iactetur in undis
et, quamcumque viam dederit Fortuna, sequatur:
sentences.l:
Aeneas, by all means, on unknown waves let him be tossed,
and, whatever way Fortune has given, let him follow:
sentences.i: Let Aeneas, if it must be, be tossed on unknown seas and follow whatever road Fortune opens to him:
sentences.n: 'sane', 'by all means, granted', concessive: Venus gives up her son to save her grandson. 'iactetur… sequatur', jussive or concessive subjunctives, 'let him be tossed… let him follow'. 'ignotis… in undis', 'on unknown waters', a sharp reversal of all the oracles that promised Italy. 'quamcumque viam dederit', 'whatever way (Fortune) shall have given', future perfect in sense (the same form is the perfect subjunctive, drawn into the mood of 'sequatur'). 'Fortuna' is personified, with a capital. Elision 'san(e) ignotis'.

sentences.t: hunc tegere et dirae valeam subducere pugnae.
sentences.l: him may I be able to shield and from dire battle to withdraw.
sentences.i: but let me have the power to shelter this boy and steal him away from the cruel battle.
sentences.n: 'hunc', 'this one', Ascanius, not Aeneas. 'valeam', 'may I be able', subjunctive of wish. 'tegere… subducere', 'to protect… to withdraw', both depending on 'valeam'. 'dirae… pugnae', dative of separation with 'subducere', 'to withdraw from the dreadful fight'; verbs of taking away often take the dative in verse. Elision 'teger(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Est Amathus, est celsa mihi Paphus atque Cythera
Idaliaeque domus:
sentences.l:
There is Amathus, there is lofty Paphus for me, and Cythera
and Idalia's house:
sentences.i: I have Amathus, I have high Paphos, and Cythera, and my house at Idalium:
sentences.n: 'Est… est… mihi', 'there is… there is to me', a dative of possession (as in 'sunt mihi'). Venus names her cult places: Amathus, Paphos and Idalium are in Cyprus, where she was worshipped above all; Cythera is the island off the southern tip of Greece where she came ashore from the sea. 'Paphus' is the Latin form of Paphos. 'Idaliae… domus', 'the house of Idalia', genitive; Idalia is another name for Idalium, and the house is her temple there. Juno will throw this list back at her in line 86. No elisions.

sentences.t:
positis inglorius armis
exigat hic aevum.
sentences.l:
his arms laid down, without glory
let him pass here his life.
sentences.i: there let him lay down his arms and live out his days without renown.
sentences.n: 'positis… armis', ablative absolute, 'his arms having been laid down'. 'inglorius', 'without glory', a heavy word for the boy destined to found Alba Longa. 'exigat… aevum', 'let him spend his lifetime', jussive subjunctive; 'exigo' here 'to drive through to the end, to pass'. 'hic', 'here', in one of her sanctuaries. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Magna dicione iubeto
Karthago premat Ausoniam:
sentences.l:
With great dominion command
Carthage to crush Ausonia:
sentences.i: Command that Carthage crush Italy beneath her mighty sway:
sentences.n: 'iubeto', the future imperative, formal and solemn, the tone of laws and decrees. 'Karthago premat', 'that Carthage press down', the subjunctive standing with 'iubeto' without 'ut'. 'Magna dicione', 'with great dominion', ablative of means. 'Ausoniam', a poetic name for Italy, from the Ausones, an old people of the south. Venus bitterly turns Jupiter's own prophecy of Carthage (line 12) upside down. No elisions.

sentences.t:
nihil urbibus inde
obstabit Tyriis.
sentences.l:
nothing to the cities from there
will stand in the way, the Tyrian ones.
sentences.i: then nothing from this quarter will stand in the way of the Tyrian cities.
sentences.n: 'nihil… obstabit', 'nothing will block', with the dative 'urbibus… Tyriis'. 'Tyriis', 'Tyrian', Carthaginian: Carthage was founded by Dido and settlers from Tyre in Phoenicia. 'inde', 'from that quarter', from Ascanius and the Trojans, once they are out of the way. The irony is heavy: without the Trojans there will be no Rome to stand against Carthage. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quid pestem evadere belli
iuvit et Argolicos medium fugisse per ignes
totque maris vastaeque exhausta pericula terrae,
dum Latium Teucri recidivaque Pergama quaerunt?
sentences.l:
What did it help to escape the plague of war,
and through the midst of the Argive fires to have fled,
and so many dangers of sea and of vast land to have drained,
while Latium the Teucrians and a Pergamum reborn seek?
sentences.i: What good has it done them to escape the pestilence of war, to have fled through the thick of the Argive fires, to have endured to the last every danger of the sea and of the wide earth, while the Trojans search for Latium and a Pergamum risen again?
sentences.n: 'Quid… iuvit', 'what did it profit', with three infinitives as subject: 'evadere', 'fugisse', and 'exhausta (esse)', 'to have drained'. 'pestem belli', 'the plague of war', the fall of Troy. 'Argolicos… ignes', 'the Argive fires', Troy burned by the Greeks; 'medium… per ignes', 'through the midst of the fires', as in Book II. 'exhausta pericula', 'dangers drained', endured to the end. 'recidiva… Pergama', 'Pergamum falling back again', a Troy rising again; Pergama, the citadel of Troy, is neuter plural. Elisions 'pest(em) evadere', 'vastaequ(e) exhausta'.

sentences.t:
Non satius cineres patriae insedisse supremos
atque solum, quo Troia fuit?
sentences.l:
Not better on the ashes of the fatherland to have settled, its last,
and the soil, where Troy was?
sentences.i: Would it not have been better to settle on the last ashes of their homeland, on the ground where Troy once stood?
sentences.n: 'Non satius (fuit)', 'was it not better', the verb left out. 'insedisse', perfect infinitive of 'insido', 'to have settled upon', taking the accusatives 'cineres… solum'. 'cineres… supremos', 'the last ashes', noun and adjective enclosing 'patriae insedisse': the final embers of the city. 'quo Troia fuit', 'where Troy was', 'fuit' with the force of 'is no more', as in Book II's 'fuimus Troes'. Elision 'patri(ae) insedisse'.

sentences.t:
Xanthum et Simoenta
redde, oro, miseris iterumque revolvere casus
da, pater, Iliacos Teucris.”
sentences.l:
Xanthus and Simois
give back, I pray, to the wretched, and again to roll through the misfortunes
grant, father, of Ilium, to the Teucrians.”
sentences.i: Give the poor Trojans back their Xanthus and their Simois, I beg you, father, and let them live through the troubles of Ilium once more.”
sentences.n: Venus's speech ends here, after forty-five lines. The Xanthus and the Simois are the two rivers of the Trojan plain. 'Simoenta', Greek accusative. 'redde', 'give back', imperative; 'oro', 'I pray', thrown in parenthetically. 'revolvere casus… da', 'grant (them) to roll back through their misfortunes', 'da' with the infinitive, a poetic construction. 'Iliacos… casus', 'the misfortunes of Ilium', framing the clause. 'miseris… Teucris', dative, 'to the unhappy Trojans'. Elisions 'Xanth(um) et', 'redd(e) oro'.

sentences.t:
Tum regia Iuno
acta furore gravi:
sentences.l:
Then royal Juno,
driven by heavy fury:
sentences.i: Then queenly Juno, goaded by a deep and bitter rage:
sentences.n: Greenough prints a half-line 62b here: the end of Venus's speech and 'Tum regia Iuno' are set as two hemistichs, and the standard numbering counts them as one line, 62. Juno breaks in within the same verse, giving Venus no pause. 'regia', 'royal', queen of the gods. 'acta furore gravi', 'driven by heavy fury', the verb of speaking left out (as in 'Iuppiter haec paucis', line 16). She has sat silent through Venus's whole speech. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Quid me alta silentia cogis
rumpere et obductum verbis volgare dolorem?
sentences.l:
“Why me deep silence do you force
to break, and a covered-over grief in words to publish?
sentences.i: “Why do you force me to break my deep silence and lay bare in words a grief long kept covered?
sentences.n: Juno's speech begins. 'alta silentia', 'deep silences', the plural poetic. 'cogis… rumpere', 'do you force (me) to break'. 'obductum… dolorem', 'grief drawn over', healed over like a wound under a scar, and now reopened. 'volgare', Greenough's spelling of 'vulgare', 'to make common, to publish'. Elisions 'm(e) alta', 'rumper(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Aenean hominum quisquam divomque subegit
bella sequi aut hostem regi se inferre Latino?
sentences.l:
Aeneas did anyone of men or gods compel
wars to pursue, or as an enemy upon King Latinus to thrust himself?
sentences.i: Did any man or any god compel Aeneas to go seeking war, or to force himself as an enemy upon King Latinus?
sentences.n: 'Aenean', Greek accusative of 'Aeneas'. 'hominum quisquam divomque', 'anyone of men and gods', 'divom' = 'divorum' again. 'subegit', 'drove, compelled', with the infinitives 'sequi' and 'inferre'. 'hostem… se inferre', 'to bring himself in as an enemy', 'hostem' predicative. 'regi… Latino', dative with 'inferre'. Juno argues that Aeneas chose his war. Elisions 'sequ(i) aut', 's(e) inferre'.

sentences.t:
Italiam petiit fatis auctoribus, esto,
Cassandrae inpulsus furiis:
sentences.l:
Italy he sought with the fates as sponsors — be it so —
driven by the frenzies of Cassandra:
sentences.i: He made for Italy with the fates to vouch for him — granted — driven on by the ravings of Cassandra:
sentences.n: 'fatis auctoribus', ablative absolute, 'the fates being his sponsors', 'auctor' the one who guarantees a transaction. 'esto', future imperative of 'sum', 'be it so', granting the point only to undercut it. 'Cassandrae… furiis', 'by the frenzies of Cassandra', Priam's daughter, the prophetess no one believed; in Book III Anchises remembers that she foretold Italy. The sneer is that the fates spoke through a madwoman. 'inpulsus' is Greenough's spelling of 'impulsus'. Elision 'Cassandr(ae) inpulsus'.

sentences.t:
num linquere castra
hortati sumus aut vitam committere ventis?
sentences.l:
surely we did not to leave the camp
urge him, or his life to entrust to the winds?
sentences.i: but did I urge him to leave his camp, or to trust his life to the winds?
sentences.n: 'num… hortati sumus', 'surely we did not urge', 'num' expecting the answer no. Juno, like Venus, speaks of herself in the plural. 'linquere castra', 'to leave the camp', as Aeneas did in Book VIII to seek allies, the very point Venus made ('Aeneas ignarus abest'). 'vitam committere ventis', 'to entrust his life to the winds', to go off by water up the Tiber. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Num puero summam belli, num credere muros
Tyrrhenamque fidem, aut gentis agitare quietas?
sentences.l:
Did we urge him to a boy the command of the war, to entrust the walls,
and Tyrrhenian loyalty, or peoples at rest, to stir up?
sentences.i: Did I urge him to hand the conduct of the war and the defence of the walls to a boy, to tamper with the loyalty of the Etruscans, or to set quiet nations in turmoil?
sentences.n: 'Num… num', 'surely (we did) not… surely not', with 'hortati sumus' carried over from line 69. 'puero', 'to a boy', Ascanius, left in command of the camp. 'summam belli', 'the sum of the war', the chief command. 'Tyrrhenam… fidem', 'Tyrrhenian good faith', the alliance with the Etruscans that Aeneas went to seek in Book VIII; 'agitare', 'to stir, to tamper with', serves both 'fidem' and 'gentis'. 'gentis… quietas', 'peoples at rest', 'gentis' an accusative plural in '-is'. Elision 'fid(em) aut'.

sentences.t:
Quis deus in fraudem, quae dura potentia nostra
egit?
sentences.l:
What god into harm, what harsh power of ours
drove him?
sentences.i: What god, what harshness of my power drove him into this mischief?
sentences.n: 'in fraudem', 'into harm, into mischief', 'fraus' in its old sense of damage or ruin rather than deceit. 'quae dura potentia nostra', 'what harsh power of mine', throwing back Venus's 'tua coniunx dura' (lines 44–45). The verb 'egit', 'drove', is held over to the next line, with a strong pause after it. No elisions.

sentences.t: Ubi hic Iuno demissave nubibus Iris?
sentences.l: Where here is Juno, or Iris sent down from the clouds?
sentences.i: Where in all this is Juno, or Iris let down from the clouds?
sentences.n: 'Ubi hic', 'where in this', what part has Juno played here. She speaks of herself by name, in mockery of Venus's charges, and answers her complaint about Iris ('actam nubibus Irim', line 38); the reader of Books V, VII and IX knows the charges are true. 'demissa nubibus', 'sent down from the clouds', ablative of separation; '-ve', 'or'. Elision 'Ub(i) hic'.

sentences.t:
Indignum est Italos Troiam circumdare flammis
nascentem et patria Turnum consistere terra,
cui Pilumnus avus, cui diva Venilia mater:
sentences.l:
Shameful it is that the Italians Troy should surround with flames
being born, and on his native land Turnus take his stand,
whose grandfather is Pilumnus, whose mother the goddess Venilia:
sentences.i: It is an outrage, is it, that Italians should ring with fire a Troy just coming to birth, and that Turnus should stand his ground on the soil of his fathers — Turnus, whose grandfather is Pilumnus, whose mother is the goddess Venilia:
sentences.n: 'Indignum est', 'it is shameful', with the accusatives and infinitives 'Italos… circumdare' and 'Turnum consistere'; Juno takes up Venus's outrage in order to mock it, and 'Troiam… nascentem' throws back her 'nascentis Troiae' (line 27). 'patria… terra', 'on his native soil', ablative of place. Pilumnus was an old Italian god of the farmstead; Venilia, a nymph. Juno's point is that Turnus too has gods in his family. 'cui… cui', dative of possession, with 'est' understood. Elisions 'Indign(um) est', 'nascent(em) et'.

sentences.t:
quid face Troianos atra vim ferre Latinis,
arva aliena iugo premere atque avertere praedas?
sentences.l:
what, that Trojans with black torch bring violence on the Latins,
the fields of others with the yoke press, and drive off plunder?
sentences.i: And what of Trojans bringing violence on the Latins with smoking torches, bending other men's fields beneath their yoke and driving off their spoil?
sentences.n: 'quid', 'what (of the fact) that', introduces more accusatives and infinitives, the accusative and infinitive of indignation (as in 'Mene… desistere', Book I): 'Troianos… ferre… premere… avertere'. 'face atra', 'with a black torch', smoky and deadly: Juno turns the charge of fire-raising back on the Trojans. 'iugo premere', 'to press with the yoke', to subdue, or to plough as if they owned the land. 'avertere praedas', 'to drive off booty', cattle carried off. Elisions 'arv(a) aliena', 'premer(e) atque', 'atqu(e) avertere'.

sentences.t:
Quid soceros legere et gremiis abducere pactas,
pacem orare manu, praefigere puppibus arma?
sentences.l:
What, to choose fathers-in-law, and from laps to lead away the betrothed,
to beg peace with the hand, to fix on the sterns arms?
sentences.i: And what of choosing fathers-in-law for themselves and carrying off brides already promised from their mothers' arms, of begging peace with the olive branch while they fix weapons on their sterns?
sentences.n: 'Quid', as before, with more infinitives of indignation. 'soceros legere', 'to choose fathers-in-law', Latinus, whose daughter Lavinia had been promised to Turnus. 'gremiis abducere pactas', 'to lead away brides already pledged from (their mothers') laps', 'pactas' the participle of 'paciscor' used as a noun. 'pacem orare manu', 'to beg peace with the hand', holding out the olive branch as the Trojan envoys did before Latinus in Book VII. 'praefigere puppibus arma', 'to fix weapons on their sterns', a sign of war. Elisions 'leger(e) et', 'pac(em) orare'.

sentences.t:
Tu potes Aenean manibus subducere Graium
proque viro nebulam et ventos obtendere inanis,
tu potes in totidem classem convertere nymphas:
sentences.l:
You can Aeneas from the hands draw away of the Greeks,
and in place of the man a mist and winds hold out, empty,
you can into as many turn the fleet, nymphs:
sentences.i: You can snatch Aeneas out of the hands of the Greeks and set a cloud and empty air before them in place of the man; you can turn a fleet into as many nymphs:
sentences.n: 'Tu potes… tu potes', anaphora, the rhythm of an attack. In Iliad 5 Aphrodite tried to carry the wounded Aeneas out of the fight, but Diomedes wounded her and she let him fall; Apollo then hid him in a dark cloud and left a phantom of him on the field. Juno gives Venus all the credit. 'Graium' = 'Graiorum'. 'proque viro', 'and in place of the man'. 'ventos… inanis', 'empty winds', accusative plural in '-is'. In Book IX the Trojan ships were turned into sea-nymphs as Turnus tried to burn them; that was the Mother of the Gods' doing, but Juno lays it at Venus's door. The Latin Library has 'et potes' in 83, which loses the second 'tu'. Elisions 'nebul(am) et', 'obtender(e) inanis'.

sentences.t: nos aliquid Rutulos contra iuvisse nefandum est?
sentences.l: that we somewhat the Rutulians in turn have helped, is it a crime?
sentences.i: and is it a crime if I in my turn have given the Rutulians some help?
sentences.n: 'nos aliquid… iuvisse', 'that we have helped somewhat', accusative and infinitive as subject of 'nefandum est', 'is it unspeakable', a sin too great to name. 'aliquid', adverbial accusative, 'to some extent'. 'Rutulos contra', best taken with 'contra' as an adverb, 'on the other side, in return', and 'Rutulos' as the object of 'iuvisse'. Elision 'nefand(um) est'.

sentences.t: Aeneas ignarus abest:
sentences.l: Aeneas, unknowing, is away:
sentences.i: Aeneas is away and knows nothing of it:
sentences.n: Juno takes Venus's own words from line 25, 'Aeneas ignarus abest', and repeats them exactly, so that she can turn them round in the next half-line. Throwing an opponent's words back at her is a favourite move of ancient oratory, and Juno does it again with Venus's list of shrines in the next line. No elisions.

sentences.t: ignarus et absit.
sentences.l: unknowing let him also be away.
sentences.i: then let him stay away and know nothing.
sentences.n: 'ignarus et absit', 'let him also stay away unknowing', jussive subjunctive; 'et' here means 'also', 'so let him'. The repetition of 'ignarus' across the pause makes the sneer: if he chose to be away, that is his own affair. No elisions.

sentences.t: Est Paphus Idaliumque tibi, sunt alta Cythera:
sentences.l: There is Paphus and Idalium for you, there is lofty Cythera:
sentences.i: You have Paphos and Idalium, you have high Cythera:
sentences.n: Juno echoes Venus's list (line 51, 'Est Amathus, est celsa mihi Paphus atque Cythera'), changing 'mihi' to 'tibi': go back to your shrines, she means, and leave Italy alone. 'tibi', dative of possession, as before. 'Idalium', neuter, the town in Cyprus. 'alta Cythera', neuter plural. No elisions.

sentences.t: quid gravidam bellis urbem et corda aspera temptas?
sentences.l: why a city pregnant with wars and rough hearts do you meddle with?
sentences.i: why meddle with a city teeming with wars, and with hearts that are hard?
sentences.n: 'quid', 'why'. 'gravidam bellis urbem', 'a city pregnant with wars', heavy with wars to come: the Latin people seen as a single state, in contrast with the soft life of Venus's island shrines. 'corda aspera', 'rough hearts', the hardy Italians. 'temptas', 'do you try, meddle with, assail'. Elisions 'urb(em) et', 'cord(a) aspera'.

sentences.t:
Nosne tibi fluxas Phrygiae res vertere fundo
conamur, nos, an miseros qui Troas Achivis
obiecit?
sentences.l:
Is it we, to your cost, the tottering fortunes of Phrygia from the foundation to overturn
who try, we? or he who the wretched Trojans to the Achaeans
threw in the way?
sentences.i: Is it I who am trying to overturn the tottering fortunes of Phrygia from their foundations — I — or the one who threw the unhappy Trojans in the path of the Greeks?
sentences.n: 'Nosne… conamur', 'is it we who try', '-ne' marking the question; 'tibi', 'to your cost', a dative of disadvantage. 'fluxas… res', 'ebbing fortunes', things already slipping away. 'vertere fundo', 'to overturn from the bottom'. 'nos, an… qui… obiecit', 'we, or he who exposed', Paris, whose theft of Helen brought the Greeks down on Troy; Juno leaves him unnamed. 'Phrygiae', 'of Phrygia', of Troy. 'Troas', Greek accusative plural; 'Achivis', dative, 'to the Achaeans', the Greeks. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quae causa fuit, consurgere in arma
Europamque Asiamque et foedera solvere furto?
sentences.l:
What cause was there, to rise up in arms
both Europe and Asia, and treaties to break by theft?
sentences.i: What was the reason that Europe and Asia rose up in arms, and the bonds of good faith were broken by a theft?
sentences.n: 'Quae causa fuit', 'what was the cause', with the infinitives 'consurgere' and 'solvere' explaining it, 'that Europe and Asia should rise…'. 'Europamque Asiamque', the double '-que', 'both Europe and Asia', Greece against Troy. 'foedera', 'compacts', the laws of hospitality that Paris broke as Menelaus's guest. 'furto', 'by a theft', the carrying off of Helen. Elisions 'consurger(e) in', 'Europamqu(e) Asiamqu(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Me duce Dardanius Spartam expugnavit adulter,
aut ego tela dedi fovive cupidine bella?
sentences.l:
With me as leader did the Dardan storm Sparta, the adulterer,
or did I give the weapons or nurse with desire the wars?
sentences.i: Was it with me to lead him that the Dardan adulterer took Sparta by storm, or I who put weapons in men's hands and fed the war with lust?
sentences.n: 'Me duce', ablative absolute, 'with me as leader': Venus, not Juno, guided Paris, since she had promised him Helen when he judged her the fairest of the goddesses, the slight Juno never forgave (Book I). 'Dardanius… adulter', 'the Dardan adulterer', Paris, the sneering noun held back to the end of the line. 'Spartam expugnavit', 'took Sparta by storm', bitter irony for a seduction. 'fovive', 'or did I foster', '-ve' 'or'. 'cupidine', 'with desire', or with Cupid, Venus's son. Elision 'Spart(am) expugnavit'.

sentences.t: Tum decuit metuisse tuis:
sentences.l: Then it was fitting to have feared for your own:
sentences.i: That was the time to fear for your people:
sentences.n: 'Tum', 'then', at the time of Paris's crime, set against 'nunc' in the next clause. 'decuit metuisse', 'it was fitting to have feared', the perfect infinitive after a past verb of propriety, common in verse with no extra sense of past time. 'tuis', 'for your own (people)', dative with 'metuere', to fear on someone's behalf. No elisions.

sentences.t:
nunc sera querelis
haud iustis adsurgis et inrita iurgia iactas.”
sentences.l:
now late with complaints
not just you rise up, and vain quarrels you hurl.”
sentences.i: now it is too late to rise up with complaints that have no justice in them and fling about idle abuse.”
sentences.n: Juno's speech ends here, and with it the debate in council. 'sera', 'late', an adjective used for an adverb, agreeing with the subject: you rise too late. 'querelis… haud iustis', 'with complaints not just', ablative of manner. 'adsurgis', 'you rise up', Greenough's spelling of 'assurgis'. 'inrita iurgia', 'useless wranglings', alliterating with 'iactas', 'you toss about'. 'inrita' is the unassimilated spelling of 'irrita'. No elisions.
